system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2203-04-29 23:27:00 to 2203-05-07 14:33:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis, neurogenic bladder with chronic Foley catheter, and a history of recurrent UTIs, was admitted for worsening leg weakness and found to have a urinary tract infection due to E. coli. He was treated with IV ampicillin-sulbactam after culture confirmed sensitivity, having initially been on cefepime. His weakness, attributed to a recrudescence of myelopathy triggered by infection, improved with treatment. A bladder stone found at the catheter tip was sent for pathology, and urology recommended outpatient cystolitholapaxy to prevent future infections. Pressure ulcers on the left hip and right buttock were managed with bedside debridement and ongoing wound care. His fluoxetine was increased for depression, and he was discharged to extended care with a seven-day course of IV antibiotics, pending follow-up for stone results, urology, neurology, and wound management.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Other and unspecified Escherichia coli [E. coli]
Major depressive affective disorder, single episode, unspecified

radiology_notes.text:
IV access needed for antibiotics.  Patient failed PICC placement bedside.

Procedure was explained to the patient.  A preprocedure timeout was performed
as per ___ protocol.

TECHNIQUE:

Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, an attempt to puncture the right
basilic vein was done, however, unsuccessful.  Following, the right brachial
vein was punctured using a micropuncture set.  The wire could not be advanced,
and even though attempt to place a micropuncture sheath was made, however,
that was also unsuccessful.  Ultrasound imaging demonstrated the vein to be
very small, and decision was made to attempt the left side.

Following, the left arm was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. 
The left brachial vein was punctured under direct ultrasound guidance using a
micropuncture set.  Ultrasound image was saved after establishing intravenous
access.  Following, a peel-away sheath was then placed over a guidewire and a
double-lumen PICC line measuring 40.5 cm in length was then advanced through
the peel-away sheath with its tip positioned in the SVC under fluoroscopic
guidance.  Position of the catheter was confirmed by fluoroscopic spot film of
the chest.  The peel-away sheath and guidewire were then removed. The catheter
was secured to the skin, flushed and sterile dressing was applied.  Patient
tolerated the procedure well without immediate complications.

IMPRESSION:
Unsuccesful right arm access.
Ultrasound of fluoroscopic-guided placement of a double-lumen PICC line via
the left brachial venous approach.  
Final internal length is 40.5 cm, with its tip positioned in the SVC, and the
line is ready for use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're in the hospital because you've been feeling weak. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been really weak since yesterday afternoon. It’s the same way I feel every time I get a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We know you’re at risk for UTIs because of your catheter. Did you notice anything different with your urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t really check it. I don’t know when the catheter was last changed. I haven’t had fevers or pain, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We sent a urine test from your current catheter. We’ve started you on an antibiotic called cefepime, based on what’s worked before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that going to be enough? I’ve had tough infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’ll get the culture results in a day or two. Then we’ll know exactly which bacteria are causing the infection and can adjust antibiotics if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back. You have two bacteria: E. coli and Enterococcus. The E. coli is resistant to several antibiotics, including ampicillin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is the cefepime still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cefepime works for this E. coli, but because of the Enterococcus, we need to add another antibiotic. We’ll start IV ampicillin for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Two antibiotics? That sounds intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but it’s important to treat both infections fully. We’ll give them IV for two weeks to make sure we clear everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where will I get the IV antibiotics? I can’t stay here that long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll place a PICC line—a special IV in your arm—so you can get antibiotics at a rehab facility. That way, you won’t need daily needle sticks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to remove your Foley catheter today. We want to see if you can empty your bladder on your own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m incontinent. I don’t control my bladder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’ll do bladder scans every few hours to check how much urine stays in. If it’s low, you can stay without a catheter, which helps prevent infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but what if I start retaining too much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then we’d consider reinserting a catheter. But for now, we’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your first bladder scan showed only 150 cc retained. That’s good. You’re not holding much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m okay without the catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. We’ll keep checking. Less catheter time means lower infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The wound on your left hip is large and deep. General surgery is coming to debride it today—clean out dead tissue to help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that going to hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll use local numbing medicine. You might feel pressure, but not sharp pain. It’s important to prevent infection and help healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The debridement went well. They removed dead tissue from your hip ulcer. Wound care will manage dressings daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it heal completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a tough wound because of your limited mobility and weight loss. Healing will take time and good nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We need to place the PICC line today. It’ll go into your arm and let you get antibiotics safely for two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It’s a common procedure. They’ll use ultrasound to guide it and make sure it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They had some trouble with the right arm, but got the PICC in through your left arm. It’s in the right place and ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Glad that’s done. So now it’s just antibiotics and waiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pretty much. We’re also watching your strength. Your weakness is likely from the infection affecting your MS.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your white count is coming down. That means the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my strength?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re moving a bit better. It’ll keep improving as the infection clears.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve lost about 50 pounds recently. Is that part of this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely due to poor appetite and chronic illness. We’re encouraging high-protein meals to help you regain strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve decided to switch your antibiotic for E. coli. Instead of cefepime, we’re starting imipenem-cilastatin because it’s more effective for this strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It covers a broader range of bacteria and is better for resistant E. coli. You’ll stay on it for the full two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ampicillin for Enterococcus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue that too. Both are needed to fully treat the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Surgery did a small bone debridement near your hip wound today to remove any infected bone fragments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More surgery? I didn’t know that was needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was minor—done under local anesthesia. It helps prevent the wound from getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Infection signs are improving, and your wound care is on track. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where am I going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To an extended care facility. They can give your IV antibiotics and manage wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but you need daily nursing for antibiotics and wound care. The facility is best for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, if it’s necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s your discharge day. You’re on two IV antibiotics for two weeks—imipenem and ampicillin—through your PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well without it. Bladder scans showed low retention. If that changes later, urology can reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the wound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dressings will be changed daily. Keep the area clean and dry. Pressure relief is key—try not to sit on that side too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my MS and depression?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Both are stable. Keep taking fluoxetine. Your weakness should keep improving as the infection clears.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—urology, neurology, and wound care. We’ll send all the details to the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling better. The team will get you transferred soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with multiple sclerosis, neurogenic bladder, and chronic indwelling Foley catheter, was admitted for generalized weakness, a known trigger for urinary tract infections in his case. He was found to have a UTI with both Escherichia coli and Enterococcus species. Initial treatment with cefepime was adjusted to imipenem-cilastatin and IV ampicillin based on culture sensitivities. A PICC line was placed for two weeks of outpatient IV antibiotics. His Foley catheter was removed, and bladder scans showed acceptable post-void residuals. He underwent surgical debridement of a stage IV left trochanteric pressure ulcer and a minor bone debridement, with ongoing wound care planned. He improved clinically and was discharged to extended care for antibiotic completion and rehabilitation.
